quiz.question: Why do next-token language models hallucinate?
options: They query a verified world model before every token
They sample locally likely continuations, which can be fluent and still false
They are forbidden from producing any string not seen in training
They only copy documents verbatim, so they cannot invent
quiz.explanation: Training and decoding optimize sequence likelihood, not a truth check. A high-probability continuation can be wrong.

quiz.question: Temperature in decoding mainly controls:
options: How many tokens fit in the context window
How peaked versus flat the next-token sampling distribution is
The tokenizer vocabulary size
Whether retrieved documents are allowed
quiz.explanation: Higher temperature flattens probabilities (more random). Lower temperature sharpens them (more greedy). It does not add knowledge.

quiz.question: Why are tokens not the same as words?
options: Billing is always one token per English word
Tokenizers split text into subword pieces; counts vary by language, code, and punctuation
One token is always one Unicode character
Whitespace is never assigned a token
quiz.explanation: Subword tokenizers merge or split pieces. Limits, truncation, and cost are in tokens, not words.

quiz.question: Putting more text into the context window mainly costs you:
options: Only local disk space on the client
Compute, latency, and usually money for every token the model must process
Nothing; unused prompt tokens are free
Only the number of words in the final answer
quiz.explanation: Included tokens are processed. Longer context raises cost and latency and can bury the relevant span.

quiz.question: RAG still fails when:
options: The retriever never surfaces the passage that actually answers the question
Adjacent chunks share a small overlap
You log which document IDs were retrieved
You cap the maximum answer length
quiz.explanation: The generator can only ground on what retrieval returns. A miss forces the model to guess.

quiz.question: A common chunking mistake is:
options: Keeping a heading with the paragraph it introduces
Splitting a definition so the term and its meaning land in different chunks
Using modest overlap between neighboring chunks
Dropping repeated boilerplate headers
quiz.explanation: If term and meaning are separated, retrieval can return the term without the meaning, and the model invents one.

quiz.question: An eval pitfall is scoring a system by:
options: Held-out gold answers for the actual task
Whether the model’s own prose says the answer “looks good,” with no task labels
Retrieval recall on a labeled corpus
Agreement with a blinded human rubric
quiz.explanation: Fluency and self-agreement are not correctness. Eval needs a target the system cannot grade-inflate.

quiz.question: Prefer RAG over fine-tuning when:
options: You only need a new output JSON schema once
Facts live in documents that change and must be citable
You want to avoid embeddings and search entirely
You cannot write a system prompt
quiz.explanation: RAG attaches living sources at inference. Fine-tuning is a poor store for facts that move.

quiz.question: Prefer changing the prompt over fine-tuning when:
options: You must bake a huge private corpus into weights
The task, format, and constraints can be stated in the input
You need a new tokenizer
You want to skip evaluation
quiz.explanation: If instructions in context are enough, prompting is cheaper and easier to reverse than a weight update.

quiz.question: Prompt injection is:
options: A GPU memory allocator bug
Untrusted text in context that tries to override the developer’s instructions
Setting temperature above 1
Using too many few-shot examples
quiz.explanation: Once attacker-controlled content is in the prompt (PDF, web page, email), it can compete with the system task.

quiz.question: Temperature near zero typically:
options: Samples more often from the long tail of tokens
Makes decoding more deterministic by favoring the highest-probability tokens
Expands the context window
Guarantees factually correct answers
quiz.explanation: Near-greedy decoding repeats high-likelihood tokens. It reduces randomness, not hallucination.

quiz.question: A model can sound confident while wrong because:
options: Token likelihood is not a calibrated score that the claim is true
Every decoded sentence is checked against a knowledge graph
Temperature is a built-in fact checker
Decoding uses symbolic proof search
quiz.explanation: Fluency and local probability track “what text usually comes next,” not “what is true.”

quiz.question: Context-window cost grows with:
options: Only the number of user accounts
Input and generated tokens the model processes (and, with attention, interactions among them)
Only images, never text
The number of CPU cores on the client laptop
quiz.explanation: You pay for tokens processed. Attention can scale worse than linear in sequence length, so long prompts are not free.

quiz.question: Which mapping is most accurate?
options: Fine-tune: changing daily prices; RAG: tone of voice; prompt: new weights
Prompt: task framing; RAG: updatable external facts; fine-tune: style, format, or domain language in weights
RAG: never use documents; prompt: train for weeks
Fine-tune: cheapest way to add one new fact tonight
quiz.explanation: Use the cheapest lever that matches the failure: instructions, documents, or behavior baked into weights.

flashcards.back: They predict likely next tokens, not verified facts. Fluency is not a truth check, so coherent text can still be false.
It rescales the next-token distribution. High = more random/diverse. Low = more greedy/deterministic. It does not add knowledge.
Subword tokenizers split or merge pieces. Cost, truncation, and context limits are in tokens. The same sentence can be more tokens in some languages or in code.
Every included token is processed. Longer context raises latency, compute, and price, and can drown the useful span in noise.
If the answering chunk is never retrieved, the generator will guess. Retrieval quality is an upper bound on grounded quality.
Make each chunk self-contained enough to answer. Overlap helps boundaries. Splitting mid-table, mid-code, or mid-definition loses meaning.
Prompt = task and constraints. RAG = living documents. Fine-tune = style/format/domain behavior in weights. Do not fine-tune to store facts that change.
Attacker-controlled content in the context tries to override the system task or hijack tools. Treat retrieved and user-supplied text as untrusted.

quiz.question: A next-token model “fills in” a plausible citation that was never retrieved. The deepest cause is:
options: The optimizer directly maximizes factual F1
Decoding continues a locally likely string even when no supporting span is in context
Temperature is a citation verifier
The tokenizer refuses unknown entity names
quiz.explanation: Without a grounding constraint, the likely continuation of “according to…” is a citation-shaped string, not a checked source.

quiz.question: You raise temperature to increase idea variety on a constrained extraction task. The usual side effect is:
options: Stricter schema adherence
More format drift and made-up fields because tail tokens get more mass
A larger context window
Automatic citation checking
quiz.explanation: Higher temperature boosts low-probability tokens. On extraction, that often means broken JSON and invented keys.

quiz.question: Two sentences have the same word count. Sentence A is English prose; B is dense code with punctuation. Token counts:
options: Must be equal because words = tokens
Often differ; code and punctuation typically consume more tokens per character
Are always smaller for code
Ignore punctuation entirely
quiz.explanation: Tokenizers over-split many symbols and identifiers. Word count is a bad proxy for cost and for what still fits.

quiz.question: You paste a 200-page manual into the prompt “so nothing is missed.” A realistic failure is:
options: Attention is free, so ranking inside the window cannot matter
You pay for all tokens and the model still under-uses the buried relevant paragraph
The window compresses unused pages to zero tokens
Injection becomes impossible
quiz.explanation: Long context is billed and processed. Relevance is not guaranteed; stuffing can hide the answer in the middle.

quiz.question: Which is a RAG failure mode, not a generator-only bug?
options: The index is stale; the retrieved “policy” was replaced last week
Temperature is 0.2 instead of 0.0
The answer is truncated at max tokens after a correct quote
The system prompt asks for bullet points
quiz.explanation: Stale, wrong, or incomplete retrieval feeds the model the wrong world. The generator may faithfully summarize the wrong doc.

quiz.question: Fixed-size chunking with no overlap most often hurts when:
options: A sentence or table row is cut so neither chunk is a useful retrieval unit
You store document IDs in metadata
You normalize Unicode
You cap chunk count per query
quiz.explanation: Boundary cuts destroy local coherence. Overlap or structure-aware splits keep the answering span intact.

quiz.question: Using an LLM-as-judge on the same model family as the system under test is risky because:
options: Judges cannot read text
Shared biases (verbosity, style, self-preference) can inflate scores without measuring the task
It always underestimates fluency
It cannot output a number
quiz.explanation: Judge models prefer familiar style and longer answers. Without gold checks, you measure likeness, not truth.

quiz.question: A product catalog changes hourly. Fine-tuning nightly on the catalog is usually worse than RAG because:
options: Weights cannot store any regularities
Retraining is slow, expensive, and still leaves a stale gap between jobs, while retrieval can read the live index
RAG cannot cite a SKU
Prompts cannot mention prices
quiz.explanation: Parametric memory lags a moving corpus. Put changing facts in a store and retrieve them.

quiz.question: You need the model to always emit a strict record format and domain shorthand. Best first lever after a prompt fails at scale:
options: RAG over random web pages
Fine-tune or distill on input→format pairs, keeping facts in retrieval if they move
Raise temperature
Disable the context window
quiz.explanation: Format and dialect are behavioral. Facts that change should stay out of weights.

quiz.question: Indirect prompt injection typically happens when:
options: The developer types a new system prompt
The model retrieves or is given an external document that contains hidden instructions
Temperature is an integer
You lower max tokens
quiz.explanation: The attacker never talks to you directly. Their payload rides in content the app fetches and concatenates.

quiz.question: A support bot answers from RAG. Users report confident wrong refund rules. First debug step:
options: Assume the generator is the only fault and immediately fine-tune
Inspect whether retrieved chunks actually contain the cited rule and whether chunk boundaries split it
Set temperature to 2
Delete the system prompt
quiz.explanation: Separate retrieval miss, split chunks, ranking, and generation. Fine-tuning will not fix a missing passage.

quiz.question: Why can “answer only from context” still hallucinate?
options: The instruction is a soft constraint; the model may still continue a likely unsupported sentence
Tokenizers delete the instruction
RAG disables next-token prediction
Temperature zero forbids all tokens not in the chunk
quiz.explanation: Natural-language rules are not hard isolation. You still need retrieval quality, citations, and refusal behavior when evidence is missing.

quiz.question: Eval on 12 hand-picked “happy path” prompts is a pitfall because:
options: Small, unrepresentative n hides retrieval misses, injection, and long-context failures
Twelve is always statistically sufficient
Hand-picked cases cannot be written down
Gold labels are illegal
quiz.explanation: You need coverage of miss, conflict, stale docs, empty retrieval, and adversarial context—not only demos that work.

quiz.question: You pay per token. Which design most directly cuts cost without shrinking the model?
options: Retrieve top-k small chunks instead of stuffing whole documents, and truncate unused history
Duplicate the same PDF in the prompt for redundancy
Raise temperature so answers are longer
Disable caching of identical prefixes
quiz.explanation: Cost tracks tokens processed. Selective context beats naive stuffing.

flashcards.back: “According to…” is a likely string even with no source in context. Require retrieved spans, or refuse. Do not trust citation-shaped text.
Low temperature for extraction and tools. Higher temperature for brainstorming. Temperature will not fix missing evidence.
Code, tables, and some languages use more tokens per character. Word limits are not token limits. Truncation can drop the answer, not the preamble.
Dumping a whole corpus into the window is slow, expensive, and easy to distract. Retrieve, rank, and keep only spans that can support the answer.
Miss, stale index, wrong ranking, query-doc mismatch, chunk split, and “cited but not entailed.” Faithful summary of the wrong chunk is still a failure.
Split on headings, functions, or table rows when you can. Keep IDs and titles in the chunk. Overlap at boundaries. Avoid orphaned numbers in tables.
Tiny n, leaked test items in prompts, LLM-as-judge bias, scoring fluency, and ignoring retrieval metrics. Measure the failure you actually ship.
Payloads hide in retrieved pages, tickets, or files. Separate untrusted content, delimit it, and never let it choose tools or exfiltrate secrets.

quiz.question: Teacher-forcing trains the model on gold prefixes, but inference is autoregressive on its own tokens. This gap contributes to hallucination because:
options: The model never sees tokens at train time
Errors compound: a slightly off prefix makes a false continuation more likely, with no external correction
Temperature becomes exactly 1 at test time always
Loss is computed on images, not text
quiz.explanation: Exposure bias plus likelihood training means the model is not trained to stop and verify after its own mistakes.

quiz.question: For a tool argument that must be a valid ID, temperature 1.0 is a poor default because:
options: High entropy sampling increases the chance of a locally likely but invalid ID string
Temperature cannot affect sampled tokens
Tool IDs are never tokenized
Temperature 1.0 disables the context
quiz.explanation: Constrained outputs want a peaked distribution or a constrained decoder. Do not sample IDs from a flat tail.

quiz.question: You have a long system prompt, retrieved chunks, and a growing chat. The hidden cost is not only the latest user line because:
options: Only new characters are billed
Typical APIs bill (and the model processes) the full prompt each turn, so history plus retrieval compounds
Cached identical prefixes are never relevant to cost
Output tokens are free
quiz.explanation: Each turn re-sends prior tokens unless you have prefix caching. Retrieval-every-turn plus long memory is a cost curve, not a constant.

quiz.question: Quadratic attention in sequence length implies that doubling a dense prompt can:
options: At most double compute in those layers, never more
Roughly quadruple attention compute, on top of already paying for twice the tokens
Leave latency unchanged
Only affect disk, not GPU time
quiz.explanation: Even with linear approximations in some stacks, naive full attention is O(n²). Long windows are a systems problem, not just a quality knob.

quiz.question: Retrieved chunk C is top-ranked and the model quotes it. The answer is still wrong. Which failure is this?
options: Citation-not-entailment: the chunk is topically related but does not support the claim
Empty retrieval
Tokenizer underflow
Temperature is NaN
quiz.explanation: Ranking ≠ support. Eval must check entailment of the claim by the cited span, not merely that a citation exists.

quiz.question: Semantic chunking that embeds sliding windows and splits on similarity drops can fail when:
options: A logical unit (API + error codes) is semantically diverse so it is split, while boilerplate is glued because it is self-similar
You store metadata
You use overlap of 10–20%
You keep titles in the chunk
quiz.explanation: Similarity is not discourse structure. Tables, specs, and code often need schema-aware splits, not embedding kinks.

quiz.question: A/B eval where the judge sees the system name and prefers the verbose variant is contaminated by:
options: Length and identity bias, not the hidden task metric
Perfect calibration
Token-free scoring
Retrieval recall
quiz.explanation: Blind, length-controlled, and gold-anchored judging. Otherwise you ship the essay that flatters the judge.

quiz.question: Test questions appear inside few-shot prompts used at eval time. The pitfall is:
options: Data leakage: you are measuring memorization of the eval items, not generalization
A required RAG feature
The only way to compute BLEU
Unrelated to contamination
quiz.explanation: Held-out means held out of prompts, indexes, and fine-tunes—not only out of the training corpus you remember.

quiz.question: When is fine-tuning the wrong tool even if RAG is “hard”?
options: You need the model to recite a policy that legal changes weekly
You need a house writing style on a stable task
You need lower latency on a fixed schema after distillation
You need the model to use domain abbreviations consistently
quiz.explanation: If the source of truth must update without a training job, keep it out of weights. Hard retrieval is still the right architecture.

quiz.question: A prompt-only fix is insufficient when:
options: The model must acquire a distributional skill (accent of a dialect, layout prior) that examples in context cannot stably teach at your latency budget
You only needed to rename a field in the instructions
A single new fact must be true tomorrow
You wanted to add one URL to retrieve
quiz.explanation: Prompts are great for tasks and constraints. They are a bad way to install a large behavioral prior under tight token budgets.

quiz.question: A defense that only strips the phrase “ignore previous instructions” is weak because:
options: Injection can be encoded, translated, role-played, or aimed at tools without that phrase
That phrase is the only known attack
Models cannot read other languages
Tools never see retrieved text
quiz.explanation: Treat untrusted content as data, constrain tools, and require confirmation for side effects. Keyword filters are bypass bait.

quiz.question: Multilingual token inequality matters in production because:
options: The same user intent can exhaust the window or the budget in one language and not another
Every language has identical bytes-per-token
Truncation always drops tokens from the end of the vocabulary, not the prompt
Cost is billed per word in every API
quiz.explanation: Tokenizers are uneven. Latency, truncation, and price become language-dependent if you think in words.

quiz.question: Hybrid search (keyword + vector) often beats vectors alone for RAG because:
options: Rare IDs, error codes, and exact names are easy for lexical match and easy for embedding models to blur
Keyword search cannot find exact strings
Embeddings always preserve identifiers
Chunking becomes unnecessary
quiz.explanation: Identifiers and rare tokens are classic embedding misses. Lexical features catch them; vectors catch paraphrases.

quiz.question: A grounded-generation eval should jointly report:
options: Answer correctness, attribution/entailment to retrieved spans, and retrieval recall—not only chat fluency
Perplexity on the system prompt
Temperature as a quality score
Parameter count of the judge
quiz.explanation: A fluent, well-cited, wrong stack can fail at retrieval, at support, or at the final claim. Measure each layer.

flashcards.back: Train on gold prefixes; infer on your own tokens. Small early errors make false but likely continuations. Nothing in the loop verifies the world.
Each turn typically processes system + retrieval + history. Prefix caching helps identical heads. Naive “keep everything” is a quadratic-feeling bill.
A top chunk can be on-topic and still not entail the claim. Score span-level entailment, not the presence of a bracketed ID.
Embedding-similarity splits can glue boilerplate and break specs. Prefer document structure; put keys, titles, and units inside the chunk.
Self-preference, verbosity, position, and identity bias. Blind the judge, control length, mix human gold, and keep a frozen eval set.
Prompt: policy of the task. RAG: changing or citable facts. Fine-tune: stable skill/style under a token budget. Mixing them up wastes money and still hallucinates.
Untrusted text and trusted instructions share one context. Delimit, minimize privileges, and require out-of-band confirmation for side-effecting tools.

flashcards.front: Tokens as the real capacity unit
flashcards.back: Windows, bills, and truncation are token-based. Words, pages, and characters will lie—especially for code and non-English text.

quiz.question: An LLM agent, at minimum, is:
options: A single classification head with no tools
A loop: the model chooses actions (often tool calls), observes results, and continues until it stops
A database trigger
A tokenizer with a larger vocabulary
quiz.explanation: The model is not the product. The product is a loop that can call tools and feed observations back in.

quiz.question: When should you usually not use an agent?
options: The task is a deterministic pipeline or one model call with a known schema
The user goal is unknown and may need several tools
You must branch on intermediate observations you cannot precompute
You need open-ended research with tool use
quiz.explanation: If the steps are known, write a workflow. Agents add latency, cost, and failure modes you do not need.

quiz.question: A tool returns 500. The agent should not:
options: Retry with backoff if the error looks transient and the tool is safe to retry
Blindly retry in a tight loop with the same side-effecting payload
Surface a bounded failure to the user after a retry budget
Record the error in the trace
quiz.explanation: Unbounded retries cause storms and duplicate side effects. Treat idempotency and budgets as part of the tool contract.

quiz.question: Which is working memory for an agent, not a long-term store?
options: The current prompt: instructions, recent observations, and scratch notes in this run
A vector index of all past tickets across months
A policy wiki in RAG
A user profile database
quiz.explanation: Working memory is what is in context this episode. Long-term stores live outside the window and must be retrieved or queried.

quiz.question: An over-permissioned tool is dangerous because:
options: The model might call it with a hallucinated argument and actually take the action
Tools cannot have side effects
Permissions only affect logging
Agents cannot call tools more than once
quiz.explanation: The blast radius is the union of tools you exposed. Least privilege is the control, not hoping the model is careful.

quiz.question: Traces for agents should record:
options: Only the final paragraph shown to the user
Each model step, tool name, arguments, results, and errors, with timings
Only GPU temperature
Only the system prompt, never tool I/O
quiz.explanation: You cannot debug a loop from the last sentence. You need the trajectory.

quiz.question: A step budget or timeout exists so that:
options: The agent cannot loop until money, time, or tools are exhausted
Temperature stays at 1
Memory is encrypted
Retrieval is disabled
quiz.explanation: Loops do not halt by magic. Cap steps, wall clock, and tokens, then fail visibly.

quiz.question: A state machine (graph) agent differs from a free-form ReAct loop because:
options: Allowed transitions are explicit; the model cannot jump to an arbitrary tool at any time
State machines cannot call tools
Free-form loops cannot observe tool output
Graphs forbid timeouts
quiz.explanation: Graphs trade flexibility for predictability. Use them when the legal paths are known.

quiz.question: Tool use requires a schema because:
options: The model must emit arguments the runtime can parse and validate before execution
Schemas disable JSON
Tools ignore types
Schemas replace authentication
quiz.explanation: Invalid arguments are a tool error. Validate before side effects.

quiz.question: A classifier plus a fixed email template is usually better than an agent when:
options: Every input maps to one of a few known actions
The next tool depends on unpredictable observations
You must browse and synthesize many unknown sources
The user goal cannot be enumerated
quiz.explanation: Closed action sets do not need a planning loop. Keep the model inside a box.

quiz.question: Retrying a “create payment” tool on timeout is risky unless:
options: The tool is idempotent or you pass an idempotency key
You retry as fast as possible
You hide the error from traces
You raise temperature
quiz.explanation: Timeouts are ambiguous. Without idempotency you may double-charge.

quiz.question: Episodic memory, in agent design, usually means:
options: Records of past runs or conversations you may retrieve later
The weights of the base model
The tokenizer merge table
GPU scratch space
quiz.explanation: Episodes are prior interactions. They are not automatically in context; you choose what to fetch.

quiz.question: Giving an agent a raw shell tool as “just in case” is a problem because:
options: It can run commands you never intended, including destructive or data-exfiltrating ones
Shells cannot return text
Models cannot emit command strings
Timeouts become infinite automatically
quiz.explanation: Broad tools convert a prompt injection or a bad plan into a real incident.

quiz.question: If you have no traces, an agent that “sometimes does the wrong tool” is hard to fix because:
options: You cannot see the arguments, observations, or which step diverged
Wrong tools never happen
Logs are illegal for agents
The loop has only one step by definition
quiz.explanation: Debugging is replay of the trajectory. Ship traces from day one.

flashcards.back: The model proposes an action, the runtime executes a tool, the observation is appended, repeat until a stop condition. No loop, no agent.

flashcards.front: When NOT to use an agent
flashcards.back: Known DAG, single LLM call, strict latency SLA, pure classify/extract. Agents cost retries, tokens, and surprise.
Distinguish transient vs permanent, validate schemas, cap retries, and require idempotency for side effects. Never retry-storm.
Working: this context. Episodic: past runs. Semantic: facts/RAG. Do not pretend the window is a database.
Expose the narrowest action (refund_order_id) not a generic SQL or shell. The model will eventually call whatever you give it.
Span every thought/action/observation with ids, latency, tokens, and errors. You debug agents from traces, not from the final chat bubble.
Cap steps, wall clock, tool time, and tokens. On exhaustion, stop with a visible failure—do not wander.
Graph: allowed edges, easier eval and safety. Free-form: flexible, harder to bound. Default to a graph when the path is known.

quiz.question: In a tool loop, the model’s “plan” is only as good as:
options: The observation it actually received; a truncated or lying tool result will steer the next call
The parameter count of the base model alone
The absence of a stop token
The color of the UI
quiz.explanation: Garbage in the observation channel becomes the next argument. Treat tool results as untrusted data too.

quiz.question: You should replace an agent with a compiled workflow when you notice:
options: The same two or three tool sequences succeed almost always
Every ticket needs a unique research path
Tools do not exist yet
Users never repeat intents
quiz.explanation: Once the policy is stable, encode it. Keep the LLM for the remaining messy slot, not the whole loop.

quiz.question: A tool schema mismatch (string vs array) should be handled by:
options: Rejecting before execution, returning a structured error the model can repair, counting against the retry budget
Executing anyway and hoping
Raising temperature and resending to the tool
Dropping traces of the bad call
quiz.explanation: Validation is cheaper than side effects. Bounded repair is fine; silent coercion is not.

quiz.question: Scratchpad vs retrieved semantic memory: which statement is right?
options: Scratchpad is in-run working notes; semantic memory is an external store you query. Mixing them without a write policy causes stale or leaked state
They are the same tensor
Scratchpad survives process death by default
Semantic memory cannot be versioned
quiz.explanation: Decide what is ephemeral, what is persisted, and who can write it. Memory without policy is just a prompt leak.

quiz.question: A “search_files(glob)” tool plus “write_file(path, contents)” together are over-permissioned if the product only needs:
options: Read a ticket and post a comment
Full repository maintenance
A migration agent with human approval already in front
A coding agent in an isolated VM you accept
quiz.explanation: Match tools to the job. Comment-posting does not require arbitrary writes.

quiz.question: A good agent trace lets you answer:
options: Which step first departed from the gold policy, with the exact arguments and observation
Only whether the user clicked like
Only total GPU hours for the company
Only the final BLEU score
quiz.explanation: Credit assignment in a loop needs step-level truth. Aggregate thumbs-up will not localize a bad tool.

quiz.question: A token budget on an agent run should include:
options: System, history, each tool observation, and all model outputs—not only the last answer
Only the user’s first sentence
Only embeddings
Only logs stored on disk
quiz.explanation: Observations can dominate cost. Budget the whole trajectory or the run will blow up on a verbose tool.

quiz.question: Free-form looping is a poor fit when:
options: Compliance requires that refunds never precede identity verification, no matter what the model wants
The user is exploring an unknown codebase
Tool order cannot be known in advance
You are prototyping a research assistant
quiz.explanation: Hard ordering and forbidden skips belong in a state machine, not in a suggestion from the model.

quiz.question: Tool timeouts should be:
options: Shorter than the remaining run budget, with a defined cancel/idempotency story
Infinite so the agent never fails
Hidden from the model so it assumes success
Always equal to one millisecond
quiz.explanation: A hung tool should not take the whole conversation down. Fail, budget, and maybe retry.

quiz.question: You log thoughts in traces. A privacy issue is:
options: Thoughts and tool args can contain user secrets and must have retention and access controls like other prod logs
Traces cannot contain text
Thoughts are always synthetic and non-sensitive
GDPR never applies to logs
quiz.explanation: Agent traces are production data. Treat them as such.

quiz.question: Parallel tool calls help latency but complicate retries because:
options: Partial success: some calls commit, others fail; you need per-call status, not one big undo
Parallelism forbids schemas
Retries become unnecessary
Traces cannot record more than one span
quiz.explanation: Fan-out needs fan-in error handling. Do not retry the whole batch if one side-effecting call already succeeded.

quiz.question: When is “just add memory” the wrong fix?
options: The failure is a missing tool permission or a bad policy, and extra history only gives the model more ways to repeat it
The user refers to something said two turns ago inside the window
You retrieve the correct profile field
You store an audit log for humans
quiz.explanation: Memory amplifies whatever policy you already have. It is not a substitute for tools, graphs, or eval.

quiz.question: A human-in-the-loop approval node is a state-machine feature. Skipping it in a free-form agent typically happens because:
options: The model can call the side-effecting tool directly if that tool is in scope
Graphs magically wrap every tool
Timeouts insert approvals
Temperature 0 inserts approvals
quiz.explanation: If the dangerous tool is callable, a free-form policy is a suggestion. Put the gate in the runtime graph.

quiz.question: A retry storm from an agent usually looks like:
options: Many identical side-effecting calls after a slow 500, multiplying load and duplicate actions
A single well-bounded backoff
A user-visible stop after N errors
Jittered exponential backoff with a cap
quiz.explanation: Agents will retry if you let them. Caps, jitter, and idempotency keys are mandatory on write tools.

flashcards.back: The next action is conditioned on tool output. Truncation, injection in results, or silent coercion will be planned over as if true.

flashcards.front: Collapse the agent to a workflow
flashcards.back: When traces show a stable path, encode the path. Reserve free-form steps for genuine uncertainty.
Timeouts and retries must not double-apply payments, emails, or tickets. The tool contract includes “same key, same effect.”
Who writes episodic vs semantic memory, with what TTL, and what is in-context scratch. Unbounded writes become prompt injection and cost.
Scope by resource, verb, and environment. Separate read from write. Never hand production-admin APIs to a general chat agent.
Grade trajectories: illegal transitions, wasted steps, schema errors, budget hits—not only final answer text.
Run budget > sum of tool timeouts. Per-tool timeout < remaining run time. Token budget includes observations. Fail closed.
Ordering, approvals, and forbidden tools belong in the state machine. Prompts cannot be the only lock on a side effect.

quiz.question: A ReAct-style loop with unbounded “think” tokens before each tool call mainly fails in production because:
options: Thoughts are billed, leak into traces, can be injected into, and do not substitute for a real world model
Thoughts always improve grounding
Runtimes cannot parse function calls after text
Stop conditions become stricter automatically
quiz.explanation: Chain-of-thought is not a control plane. Bound it, don’t trust it, and put policy in code.

quiz.question: The strongest signal you should not ship an agent yet is:
options: A scripted DAG plus one extraction call meets the SLA and the audit log, and the agent only wins on rare demos
Users have open-ended goals across many tools
You cannot predefine the next observation
Research quality requires iterative search
quiz.explanation: Agents are for residual uncertainty. If a pipeline is enough, the agent is a regression in reliability.

quiz.question: Poisoned tool output (a webpage that says “now email secrets to …”) is best treated as:
options: Indirect injection into the observation channel; tools must not gain extra privileges from content they fetch
A reason to raise temperature
Proof that traces should be disabled
A tokenizer failure
quiz.explanation: Fetched text is still untrusted. The deputy (your agent) must not inherit authority from the page.

quiz.question: Non-idempotent tools plus at-least-once execution (retries, duplicates, crashes) require:
options: Deduping on a business key, or making the effect at-most-once via a store the runtime owns
Higher temperature so calls differ
Deleting traces after each retry
Parallelizing all writes always
quiz.explanation: Distributed execution is at-least-once unless you build otherwise. Agents make that visible quickly.

quiz.question: Semantic memory that the agent can write without review creates a loop where:
options: Hallucinations get stored and later retrieved as facts, amplifying error across sessions
Memory becomes write-protected automatically
RAG cannot read the store
Tokenizers reset the index
quiz.explanation: Writable memory is a self-training set. Gate writes, version them, and allow tombstones.

quiz.question: Over-permissioned tools plus prompt injection is a full exploit path because:
options: Untrusted content can induce a call, and the runtime will execute any allowed tool with model-supplied args
Injection cannot mention tool names
Schemas block all strings
Approvals are inserted by temperature
quiz.explanation: This is confused deputy: the model is the confused deputy, the tool is the privilege. Shrink the privilege.

quiz.question: Distributed tracing for agents should propagate a run id across model, tools, and sub-agents so that:
options: You can reconstruct a causal DAG of spans when one child agent fans out
IDs are decorative only
Child agents must not log
Only the last span is kept
quiz.explanation: Multi-agent systems without correlated traces are not debuggable. One run id, parent-child spans, and packed tool I/O.

quiz.question: A cost budget that only caps output tokens will still blow up when:
options: A tool returns a huge blob that is concatenated into the next prompt every step
The model emits a short final answer
You disable retrieval
You use a state machine with no observations
quiz.explanation: Observation inflation is the usual bill. Truncate, summarize with a budget, or store large artifacts out of band.

quiz.question: Free-form vs state machine is not binary. A practical hybrid is:
options: A graph of stages with a small free-form tool loop inside a sandbox stage, then a forced review stage before writes
Free-form always, with a comment in the prompt about stages
A graph that never calls a model
No timeouts in hybrid mode
quiz.explanation: Put uncertainty in a cage. Keep irreversible actions on explicit edges.

quiz.question: Eval that only scores the final user-visible answer misses:
options: Illegal tool use, secret leakage in args, wasted steps, and near-miss policy violations that did not reach the user this time
Whether the paragraph rhymes
The tokenizer version
The color scheme
quiz.explanation: Safety and cost live on the trajectory. Final-answer eval is necessary and not sufficient.

quiz.question: A stop condition “when the model says DONE” is weak because:
options: The model can emit DONE early, late, or in a tool argument; the runtime needs an explicit halt (budget, graph terminal, or structured stop)
DONE is parsed by GPUs directly
Stop tokens cannot be configured
Agents never over-talk
quiz.explanation: Halt is a runtime property. Natural language is a hint.

quiz.question: Retrying a read-only search is usually safer than retrying a write. The precise reason is:
options: Reads are typically idempotent; writes often are not, so error class must gate retry policy per tool
Writes cannot fail
Reads never time out
Search cannot be cached
quiz.explanation: Annotate tools: retryable, side-effecting, confirmation-required. One global retry wrapper is how you duplicate writes.

quiz.question: Passing the entire raw trace back into the next prompt as “memory” is costly and unsafe because:
options: It repeats secrets, injections, and failed plans, multiplying tokens and giving old payloads another chance
Traces contain no text
Prompts cannot include JSON
Budgets ignore concatenated traces
quiz.explanation: Summarize or select memory on purpose. The trace is for operators; the prompt is a curated working set.

quiz.question: A state machine whose every node is “LLM decides any tool” has collapsed into free-form. To keep the graph meaningful you must:
options: Restrict the tool set and allowed successors per node, with runtime enforcement—not only a prompt that lists them
Name the nodes poetically
Increase temperature at terminals
Remove traces at graph edges
quiz.explanation: If every edge exists, you do not have a state machine. Enforcement is in the dispatcher.

flashcards.back: Tools, graphs, budgets, and validators are the control plane. The model proposes. If a constraint matters, do not leave it in prose.
Ship the cheapest reliable machine: software, then one LLM call, then a graph, then a free-form loop. Each step up spends reliability.
Tool results are an attack surface. Sanitize, delimit, and never let fetched text expand the allowed tool set.
Unreviewed writes turn one hallucination into future retrieval “truth.” Version, gate, and decay memory.
Injection + a powerful tool is RCE-shaped. Scope credentials per tool, per tenant, per environment. Confirm irreversible calls.
Illegal transition rate, retry density, tokens per successful task, time-to-halt, secret-in-args rate. Final accuracy hides these.
Huge tool payloads dominate tokens and can hide the goal. Store blobs by reference; put summaries in context with a hard cap.
Outer state machine for policy. Inner bounded loop for local search. Terminal nodes for writes. Runtime halt, not “please stop.”
